analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated trust fund, paid by taxing corporate offshore income, to fix drinking water and sewer systems.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2017 with 40 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to four House committees, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a federal trust fund of up to $34.85 billion a year for water and sewer projects, funded entirely by ending a tax break that lets U.S.-owned foreign subsidiaries keep their overseas profits untaxed. The money would flow to state clean-water and drinking-water loan funds, lead-pipe and lead-free school drinking water grants, septic system repair grants, rural household water wells, and technical help for small towns and tribal governments. It also nudges water systems toward public ownership and requires strong labor standards on funded construction.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with unsafe drinking water — especially lead-exposed families, schoolchildren, low-income families facing water shutoffs, residents on failing septic systems, rural households without water wells, tribal communities, and small towns that cannot afford repairs. Union construction workers would benefit from the project labor agreement requirements. Publicly owned water systems would gain funding and potential acquisitions of private systems.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with unsafe or unaffordable water

how_it_helps.text: Creates a trust fund, appropriated automatically without yearly votes, allocating 45% to clean-water state revolving funds and 43.5% to drinking-water revolving funds, with the rest split among pollution-control, monitoring, tribal, and rural well grants [S3] [S2].
Requires EPA to establish a grant program so local schools can replace drinking water fountains and coolers with lead-free fixtures and test school drinking water for lead [S3] [S2].

Allows drinking-water revolving fund money to buy privately owned water systems — even from an unwilling seller — and requires grants to homeowners to replace lead service lines on private property [S3].

Establishes a grant program to help homeowners repair, replace, or upgrade septic tanks and drainage fields, and makes permanent and expands a rural household water well grant program to $348.5 million a year [S3].

Requires EPA to study water affordability nationwide, including rate increases, shutoffs for unpaid bills, and discriminatory practices by water and sewer providers, with a report to Congress within one year [S3].
Requires states receiving revolving fund money to permit and, to the extent practicable, use project labor agreements on funded construction, and preserves prevailing-wage rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: U.S. multinational corporations: the bill ends tax deferral on their controlled foreign subsidiaries' foreign income and directs the resulting revenue to the trust fund, up to $34.85 billion per year. Their shareholders would ultimately bear that cost. Nonunion construction contractors could face reduced access to publicly funded water projects under the project labor agreement rules.

drawbacks.text: The funding mechanism is a broad tax increase on U.S.-owned foreign subsidiaries: it redefines subpart F income to include essentially all of a controlled foreign corporation's foreign-derived income, ending deferral on those earnings up to $34.85 billion a year [S3] [S2].

Revolving fund money could be used to buy a privately owned water or sewage treatment works 'from a willing or unwilling seller,' which is a significant intervention against private water utility owners [S3].

States would have to bar most revolving-fund assistance for projects benefiting new communities, lots, or subdivisions, and school districts and small utilities would still bear remaining costs and the administrative burden of compliance and testing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and concrete: lead-free school water, lead service line replacement, septic and rural well repair, and a stable funding stream for systems most communities cannot afford on their own. The main costs fall on multinational corporations and their shareholders through higher taxes, plus a possible modest increase in construction costs from labor requirements. On balance the bill is a large, targeted public investment paid for by closing an offshore tax preference.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and three subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on March 22, 2017, with 21 additional original cosponsors [S1] [S3].

It was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Agriculture Committees, and then to the Water Resources and Environment, Environment, and Commodity Exchanges, Energy, and Credit subcommittees [S5].
Forty Democrats had cosponsored the bill, but no further action was recorded after the April 11, 2017 subcommittee referral [S4] [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019 without any vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries are better off because the offshore tax change never happened, and privately owned water utilities avoided a funding stream that could have bought out their systems. Communities with lead pipes, failing septic systems, and unaffordable water bills gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 21 original cosponsors on introduction day

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Controlled committee scheduling and the House floor calendar in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after subcommittee referral; no markup or floor vote was ever scheduled before Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsor appears in the record, and the Republican-controlled House took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: U.S. multinational corporations with foreign subsidiaries
industries.note: The bill would end tax deferral on their foreign subsidiaries' income, up to $34.85 billion a year, to pay for water infrastructure. Their avoidance of that tax is the direct cost to the public benefit.

industries.industry: Privately owned water and wastewater utilities
industries.note: State revolving funds could be used to purchase privately owned treatment works and community water systems even from an unwilling seller, and most new-subdivision projects would lose funding. Publicly financed buyouts of private systems directly threaten the industry's asset base.

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction contractors and pipe manufacturers
industries.note: Up to $34.85 billion a year of new spending, a mandate for American-made materials, and prevailing wage and project labor agreement requirements would channel money toward construction trades — with union contractors gaining the most.

industries.industry: Septic and onsite wastewater service providers and well drillers
industries.note: New federal grants would pay homeowners to repair, replace, or upgrade septic systems, and the rural household water well program would grow roughly seventyfold to $348.5 million a year.
